html_source:
The many print editions of Ulysses contain literally thousands of textual variants. The text of this site does not reproduce that of any print version. It represents one person's ongoing effort to take account of differences in various editions and provide a good reading version of the novel. But for people who wish to use the site in conjunction with a physical book, buttons divide the continuous scrollable text into the discrete pages found in five different printed texts. Only pagination is reproduced, not lineation.

First Edition (1922) reproduces the pages of the Shakespeare and Company edition, reprinted in recent years as an Orchises Press hardcover facsimile and Oxford University Press and Dover Publications paperbacks.

Wordsworth Edition (1932) reproduces the pages of the Wordsworth Editions paperback based on the first Odyssey Press edition.

Alma Classics Edition (1939) reproduces the pages of hardcover and paperback books printed by Alma Classics Ltd., using the fourth and final Odyssey Press edition.

Modern Library Edition (1961) reproduces the pages of the re-edited Random House edition of 1961, sold as Modern Library hardcovers and Vintage paperbacks.

Gabler Edition (1986) reproduces the pages of Random House hardcover books and Vintage paperbacks based on Hans Walter Gabler's 1984 three-volume Garland edition.

The Gabler Ulysses, touted at its release as "the corrected text" but strongly challenged soon afterward by John Kidd, is still seen by many professional Joyceans as the best available version—no doubt in part because its line numbering makes citation easy. I am skeptical of claims that this is a reader's best option, both because of what seem to me the questionable literary merit of many of its choices and because it so often privileges early textual variants over ones ratified later in the publication history. When an artist revises something, it is usually because he thinks he can do better. When he publishes his revisions, it is usually because he thinks he has succeeded. Rather than believing that early drafts hold the key to Joyce's intentions, I prefer to trust the process by which the errata-riddled text of 1922 was slowly improved in printings that he authorized through the 1930s. Still, it is undeniable that the Gabler team cleaned up many, many remaining flaws in those texts. Because of the importance of this edition, and because of my resistance to what seems a scholarly consensus about its value, many of my notes offer opinions about its choices—good, bad, and indifferent.


John Hunt
